questions.q: What is the grain declared for this capstone's fact table?
options: One row per purchase order line — one row per product ordered on one purchase order
One row per vendor per year
One row per purchase order, summarizing all its lines
One row per product, regardless of how many times it was ordered
questions.explain: The grain maps directly onto Purchasing.PurchaseOrderDetail: one real row per (PurchaseOrderID, PurchaseOrderDetailID) pair — declared first, before any dimension or fact decision.

questions.q: Why is DimVendor designed as SCD Type 2 rather than Type 1?
options: A vendor's CreditRating and PreferredVendorStatus genuinely change over time, and the warehouse needs to know what a vendor's status was on the order date, not just what it is today
Type 2 is required for every dimension in every warehouse
Purchasing.Vendor has no ModifiedDate column
Vendors never change, so history tracking is unnecessary but required anyway
questions.explain: Tracking a vendor's status as of the order date — not just its current value — is exactly the kind of historical accuracy SCD Type 2 exists to preserve.

questions.q: Why is DimProduct described as a conformed dimension in this design?
options: It's built with the same attribute names and definition a sales-side fact table would use, so both a purchasing fact and a future sales fact could join to the exact same governed dimension
Because Production.Product is the only table in the database
Because conformed dimensions must always use SCD Type 2
Because it has no relationship to any other fact table
questions.explain: Lesson 15's conformed dimension concept means one governed definition of "product" reused unchanged across fact tables, rather than a separate, inconsistent product table for each one.

questions.q: Why is this fact table classified as an accumulating snapshot rather than a plain transaction fact?
options: A purchase order line's ReceivedQty and RejectedQty update in place as it moves through a lifecycle of milestones, instead of being written once and left immutable
Because accumulating snapshots are always used for purchasing data by definition
Because the fact table has more than five columns
Because Purchasing.PurchaseOrderDetail has no OrderQty column
questions.explain: A plain transaction fact row never changes after insert. This row's ReceivedQty and RejectedQty genuinely update as deliveries happen — the defining behavior of an accumulating snapshot fact table.

questions.q: Why do PurchaseOrderID, RevisionNumber, and Status ride directly on the fact table instead of getting their own dimension table?
options: They identify the order itself rather than describing a vendor, product, or date — that makes them degenerate dimensions
Because SQL Server does not allow dimension tables for numeric identifiers
Because they are measures, not identifying attributes
Because there is no room left in the database for another table
questions.explain: Lesson 14's degenerate dimension concept covers exactly this case — an identifying attribute like an order number kept on the fact table itself rather than modeled as a separate dimension.
